554.title: Not ten thousand years
554.hook: don't act as if you'll live ten thousand years; while you can, be good (Meditations 4.17)
554.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius use Meditations 4.17 as a prompt to stop postponing small kindnesses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: take away the opinion. Your line was take away the label. When something stung, could you split the event from the label? Day five hundred fifty-four.

Ten thousand years. That's the number Marcus Aurelius chose, and it's meant to be absurd. Nobody plans on living that long. And yet a thank-you waits a season, then a year. An apology stays ready in the head and never reaches the mouth. A visit to an aunt who keeps saying come anytime slides to some later month, as though later were endless. In the seventeenth entry of book four, Marcus wrote himself a reminder short enough to fit on a sticky note. Today: not ten thousand years.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND YEARS.` → `AS THOUGH LATER WERE ENDLESS.` → `NOT TEN THOUSAND YEARS.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's 1862 translation it reads: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good." Three sentences. A warning, a fact, and an instruction. Second, ten thousand years. That number is the joke inside the warning. Marcus isn't accusing himself of a belief. He's accusing himself of a habit: putting off the good because there always seems to be more time. Third, death hangs over you. Marcus doesn't say this to frighten himself. Stoic writers kept death in view on purpose, as a way of sorting what matters from what doesn't. If this might be the last week, the thank-you note moves up, and the argument about the thermostat moves down. Fourth, while you can, be good. Notice he doesn't say be productive, or be famous, or finish your list. He says be good. And he puts a condition on it: while it is in your power. Not when you're less busy. Not when the kids are grown. Not when you've earned a rest. The good you've been saving isn't kept somewhere safe. It's quietly expiring. Here's the Tuesday version. Think of one good act you've been holding for later. Then ask: is later actually promised? Marcus's answer, in three short sentences, was no.
screen: `A WARNING, A FACT, AN INSTRUCTION.` · `NOT A BELIEF, A HABIT.` · `DEATH IN VIEW, TO SORT WHAT MATTERS.` · `WHILE IT IS IN YOUR POWER.` · then, large: `BE GOOD WHILE I CAN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the number ten thousand sit there for a moment, and smile at it if you like. Then come back to this one hour. Who will you see in it? A coworker, a child, a stranger at the counter, a voice on the phone. Choose one. Ask quietly: what would being good to them look like, in the next hour? Something small: a real thank-you, full attention, a patient answer. Picture doing it. The bell holds the time.
Not ten thousand years. Marcus warns himself not to act as if life were endless: while it's in your power, be good. Today's word.
Your line: be good while I can. Do one good thing today for whoever is in front of you, without waiting for a better moment. Day five hundred fifty-four.

555.title: Time gained
555.hook: how much time you gain by not watching what your neighbor says or does (Meditations 4.18)
555.carry: run straight along the line, without swerving
555.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 4.18 by skipping one habit of checking on others, such as a feed, and spending the time on their own work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not ten thousand years. Your line was be good while I can. Which good thing did you stop saving for later? Day five hundred fifty-five.

A woman stands at her kitchen window, coffee going cold. Across the street, the neighbors have a new car. She notices the color, guesses the price, wonders how they afford it, remembers what her sister said about them, and then checks the clock. Twenty minutes, gone, on a life that isn't hers. Marcus Aurelius knew the habit long before anyone carried a window onto other lives in their pocket. And he did the accounting. Today: time gained.
screen: `A NEIGHBOR'S NEW CAR.` → `TWENTY MINUTES, GONE.` → `TIME GAINED.`

segments.voice: First, the sum. How much leisure he gains, Marcus writes in the eighteenth entry of book four, who doesn't look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only at what he himself is doing, so that it may be just and holy. The Greek word is euscholia, good leisure: time that's free. Watching others spends it. Second, not their business, yours. Marcus isn't saying ignore people or stop caring. He's saying stop monitoring. Monitoring means checking what others are up to so you can compare, judge or feel better or worse. It costs time, and it buys almost nothing you can use. Third, look at your own work. The attention you take back goes to one question: is what I'm doing just? A carpenter looking at the next bench all day doesn't build a better chair. Fourth, run straight. Marcus finishes with an image from the racetrack. Don't look around at the dark character of others, he says, but run straight along the line, without swerving. A runner who keeps glancing sideways loses ground. Here's the Tuesday version. Some of the time we wish we had may already be in the day, leaking out sideways into other people's cars and kitchens and arguments. Close that leak, even partly, and the minutes come back.
screen: `HOW MUCH LEISURE HE GAINS.` · `STOP MONITORING.` · `IS WHAT I'M DOING JUST?` · `RUN STRAIGHT ALONG THE LINE.` · then, large: `TIME GAINED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of the place where you most often watch other people: a feed, a group chat, a coworker's desk, a neighbor's driveway. Picture yourself reaching for it today, the way you usually do. Now picture pausing, and turning your attention back to your own next task instead. Notice the minutes you just kept. Decide on one time today when you'll skip that look. The bell holds the time.
Time gained. Marcus says how much leisure you gain by not watching what your neighbor says, does or thinks, and only seeing that your own acts are just. Today's word.
Your line: run straight along the line, without swerving. Skip one comparison scroll today, and spend those minutes on something of your own. Day five hundred fifty-five.

556.title: Fame forgets
556.hook: everyone who remembers you will soon die too (Meditations 4.19)
556.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes answer Meditations 4.19 with anonymous acts: a good deed done so that no one will know who did it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: time gained. Your line was run straight along the line, without swerving. Which comparison did you skip, and where did those minutes go instead? Day five hundred fifty-six.
screen: `RUN STRAIGHT ALONG THE LINE, WITHOUT SWERVING.`

segments.voice: Name your great-grandparents. All eight of them. Try it, without looking anything up. These were people who worked, loved, worried about money, told jokes at dinner, and were, for a while, the center of somebody's world. Three generations on, some of their names have slipped even from their own family. Marcus Aurelius, a man whose face was stamped on coins across an empire, did that same arithmetic about himself. And he used it to loosen the grip of wanting to be remembered. Today: fame forgets.
screen: `NAME ALL EIGHT GREAT-GRANDPARENTS.` → `THREE GENERATIONS LATER.` → `FAME FORGETS.`

segments.voice: First, the chain of the forgetting. In the nineteenth entry of book four Marcus writes about the person who longs to be remembered after death. They don't stop to think, he says, that every one of those who remember them will soon die too, and then those who come after, until the whole memory goes out, passed from one person to the next, through people who admire and then die. Second, suppose they don't die. Then Marcus pushes further. Suppose the people who remember you were immortal, and the memory too. What would that be to you? You'd be gone. Praise can't reach the dead. Third, even praise now. And to the living, he asks, what is praise, except for some practical use? It's information at best. It doesn't make the act better or worse. Fourth, no credit. So what's left is the act itself. If you do good to be remembered, you're building on something that will dissolve. If you do it because it's good, it's complete the moment it's done. This can sound bleak. But look at the questions it answers: will anyone notice, will this count, will they know it was me? Marcus sets them down. In the end, nobody will remember. So the good thing can be done without an audience, the way a great-grandmother might once have fed a neighbor's child and never written it down. Her name may be gone. The meal was still eaten.
screen: `EVERYONE WHO REMEMBERS WILL DIE TOO.` · `EVEN IF THEY DIDN'T, WHAT IS IT TO YOU?` · `PRAISE DOESN'T CHANGE THE ACT.` · `THE ACT IS COMPLETE WHEN DONE.` · then, large: `NO CREDIT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one person in your family line whose name you don't know, someone two or three generations back. Picture them at the end of an ordinary day, having done some small good nobody wrote down. Let them be uncredited and complete. Then choose one thing you could do today for no credit: something nobody will thank you for, or know was you. The bell holds the time.
Fame forgets. Marcus notes that everyone who remembers you will die too; so do good for its own sake, complete without credit. Today's word.
Your line: no credit. Do one good thing today that nobody will know was you. Day five hundred fifty-six.

557.title: The emerald
557.hook: is an emerald worse if no one praises it? (Meditations 4.20)
557.carry: an honest answer in an empty room
557.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes recall the emerald of Meditations 4.20 after doing something good, letting it stand without checking for anyone's reaction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fame forgets. Your line was no credit. What good thing did you do that nobody knows was you? Day five hundred fifty-seven.

Deep in a mountain in Colombia, there's an emerald nobody has found. It has been green for millions of years in the dark. No jeweler has held it up to the light. No one has said, oh, look at that. Is it any less green? Marcus Aurelius asked almost exactly that question, in the very next entry after the one on fame. Yesterday was about being remembered. Today is quieter: whether a good thing needs to be seen at all. Today: the emerald.
screen: `AN EMERALD NOBODY HAS FOUND.` → `IS IT ANY LESS GREEN?` → `THE EMERALD.`

segments.voice: First, beautiful in itself. In the twentieth entry of book four Marcus writes that everything beautiful is beautiful on its own, and complete in itself. Praise is not part of it. A thing isn't made worse or better by being praised. Second, the list. Then he gets wonderfully specific. Is an emerald made worse, he asks, if it isn't praised? What about gold, or ivory, or purple dye? A lyre? A small knife? A flower? A shrub? You can almost picture him glancing around the room. None of these changes color when someone walks past without comment. Third, the real point. Marcus says this holds for objects and works of art, and even more for what is truly beautiful: law, truth, kindness, modesty. Which of these, he asks, is beautiful because it's praised, or spoiled because it's blamed? An honest answer given in an empty room is just as honest. A kindness nobody saw is just as kind. Fourth, letting it go unpraised. Here's the practice hidden in the question. Most of us, after doing something good, wait a little for the reaction. The text back. The thank-you. The like. When it doesn't come, the good thing seems to dim. Marcus says it didn't dim. It was finished, and green, and whole, before anyone looked. That's not an argument against thanking people. Gratitude is a good of its own. It's an argument against needing it, against letting the value of your work sit in someone else's hands.
screen: `BEAUTIFUL IN ITSELF, COMPLETE.` · `AN EMERALD, A LYRE, A FLOWER.` · `LAW, TRUTH, KINDNESS, MODESTY.` · `IT WAS WHOLE BEFORE ANYONE LOOKED.` · then, large: `THE EMERALD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look at one ordinary thing near you: a cup, a plant, the grain of a table, your own hand. Nobody is admiring it right now. Look at it the way Marcus looks at his emerald, as complete on its own. Then think of one good thing in your day that went by without a word: a meal, a job done right, a patient reply. Notice if part of you is still waiting for the reaction. Set it beside the cup. Both whole. Neither waiting. The bell holds the time.
The emerald. Marcus asks whether an emerald is worse if no one praises it: what's good is complete in itself, praised or not. Today's word.
Your line: an honest answer in an empty room. When you finish something today, skip checking for the reaction. Look at the work once yourself, and call it whole. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

558.title: Do less
558.hook: to be at peace, do few things, and only what's necessary (Meditations 4.24)
558.carry: ask who actually needs me now
558.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use the question from Meditations 4.24, 'is this one of the unnecessary things?', to trim their lists and their replies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the emerald. Your line was an honest answer in an empty room. Which good thing did you let go unpraised, and did you stop yourself checking for the reaction? Day five hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `AN HONEST ANSWER IN AN EMPTY ROOM.`

segments.voice: Look at your to-do list. Not the one you wrote, the one in your head. Reply to that. Look into this. Weigh in on the group chat. Have an opinion about the news. Check the thing you already checked. It's a long list, and it's hard to say which items actually matter. Marcus Aurelius had more on his plate than most, and in the twenty-fourth entry of book four he passed on an old piece of advice that sounds almost like permission. Today: do less.
screen: `THE LIST IN YOUR HEAD.` → `WHICH ONES ACTUALLY MATTER?` → `DO LESS.`

segments.voice: First, an old saying. Do few things, says the philosopher, if you want to be at peace. Marcus doesn't name him. Readers usually identify him as Democritus, an earlier Greek thinker who wrote about cheerful calm. Second, Marcus improves it. Wouldn't it be better, he asks, to say: do what's necessary, and what the reason of a social creature requires, and in the way it requires? That brings a double peace: the peace of doing things well, and the peace of doing few. So it isn't just fewer. It's fewer and better. Third, most of it isn't needed. Then the hard sentence. Most of what we say and do, Marcus writes, isn't necessary. Take it away, and you'll have more leisure and less disturbance. So at every moment, ask yourself: is this one of the unnecessary things? Fourth, unnecessary thoughts too. And he goes one step deeper. Cut the unnecessary thoughts, he says, because then the unnecessary actions that follow them won't happen either. The extra reply starts as an extra thought. The extra worry starts as one more what-if. This isn't laziness. It's triage. A doctor in a crowded room doesn't treat everyone at once; she asks who actually needs her now. Do less isn't a mood. It's a question, asked often, with an honest answer: is this one of the necessary things, or not?
screen: `DO FEW THINGS, SAYS THE PHILOSOPHER.` · `DO WHAT'S NECESSARY, AND DO IT WELL.` · `IS THIS ONE OF THE UNNECESSARY THINGS?` · `CUT THE UNNECESSARY THOUGHTS TOO.` · then, large: `DO LESS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring up today's list, written or unwritten. Go through it slowly, one item at a time, and ask Marcus's question of each: is this necessary? Some are. Some clearly aren't. Pick one that isn't, and cross it off, on paper or in your mind. Notice what happens, if anything, when it goes. That's the kind of peace the old saying was after. The bell holds the time.
Do less. Marcus takes an old philosopher's advice, do few things, and sharpens it: do what's necessary, do it well, and drop the rest. Today's word.
Your line: ask who actually needs me now. Cross off one task today that isn't needed, and catch one unnecessary thought before it becomes an action. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

559.title: The time of Vespasian
559.hook: picture Vespasian's age: marrying, farming, flattering, all gone (Meditations 4.32)
559.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes picture their own town a century ago, as in Meditations 4.32, to see their present worries at their true size.

segments.voice: Yesterday: do less. Your line was ask who actually needs me now. Which task did you cross off, and did anything bad actually happen? Day five hundred fifty-nine.

Find an old photograph of your street, or your town's main square, from about a hundred years ago. Look at the people in it. A man in a hat hurrying somewhere. Two women talking outside a shop. A boy with a bicycle. Each of them was in the middle of something urgent: a debt, a crush, a quarrel with a brother. Every one of those urgencies is finished now. Marcus Aurelius did this exercise without photographs, using an emperor from an earlier generation of Rome. Today: the time of Vespasian.
screen: `A PHOTO OF YOUR STREET, 100 YEARS AGO.` → `EVERYONE IN IT, IN A HURRY.` → `THE TIME OF VESPASIAN.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. Think of the times of Vespasian, Marcus writes in the thirty-second entry of book four. Vespasian was an emperor from before Marcus's time. Second, the list. And what do you see? People marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting wars, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, being stubbornly proud, suspecting, plotting, wishing others dead, grumbling at the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for high office and for power. It's a list of everything people did then, and everything they do now. Third, all gone. And that whole life of theirs, Marcus says, no longer exists anywhere. Then he does it again, with the emperor Trajan's time, a little closer. Same list. Also gone. Fourth, why look. Marcus isn't doing this to feel gloomy or superior. He's doing it to measure. The quarrel that feels enormous this week is the same size as the quarrels in Vespasian's Rome. The flattering, the plotting, the grumbling: all of it went the way of the man in the hat. Marcus says to look at how many people threw themselves into these things, and then fell, and came apart. What lasts, for him, is not the outcome of the hurry. It's whether, in the middle of it, a person kept to what is right. The exercise shrinks the hurry and leaves the goodness the same size. That's the trade. The worries get smaller. Character doesn't.
screen: `THINK OF THE TIMES OF VESPASIAN.` · `MARRYING, FARMING, FLATTERING, PLOTTING.` · `THAT WHOLE LIFE IS GONE.` · `IT SHRINKS THE HURRY, NOT THE GOOD.` · then, large: `ALL GONE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture the place you live, a century ago. The same ground, different buildings. People walking, working, worrying, each one sure their worry was the big one. Watch them for a few breaths. Then let the picture fade, the way it has. Now bring up one worry of your own and set it among them. Notice its size there. What's left that still matters? The bell holds the time.
Vespasian. Marcus pictures Vespasian's Rome, marrying, farming, flattering, plotting, and notes that all of it is gone. Today's word.
Your line: all gone. When something feels urgent today, picture it in a hundred-year-old photograph, and see what size it becomes. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

560.title: The headland
560.hook: be like the headland the waves break on; it stands, and the water settles (Meditations 4.49)
560.carry: spray flies up and falls back
560.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often call up the headland of Meditations 4.49 in conflict, staying steady and letting another person's anger spend itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vespasian. Your line was all gone. What urgent thing shrank when you put it in a hundred-year-old photograph? Day five hundred sixty, the end of a week.

Stand on a rocky point on any coast in a storm and watch. The waves come in gray and enormous, one after another, and hit the rock with a sound like a slammed door. Spray flies up and falls back. And then the water slides back, foaming, and goes quiet in the little cove behind the point. The rock hasn't moved. It hasn't fought. It just stood there, and the sea calmed itself around it. Marcus Aurelius saw that picture and kept it. Today: the headland.
screen: `A ROCKY POINT IN A STORM.` → `THE ROCK HASN'T MOVED.` → `THE HEADLAND.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The forty-ninth entry of book four opens, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it." A promontory is a headland: high land running out into the sea. Second, continually. Notice the word. The waves don't stop because the rock is steady. They keep coming. Marcus isn't promising a life without trouble. He expects the waves. Third, it stands, and the water settles. The rock doesn't attack the sea or argue with it. It doesn't need to. By staying where it is, it gives the water nothing to push against, and the fury spends itself and falls quiet. The angry customer, the relative on the phone, the news that crashes in all morning: the headland doesn't break them. It just doesn't move. Fourth, the week. Look back at what this week built. Be good while I can: don't save the good for later. Time gained: stop monitoring others. No credit: do good without an audience. The emerald: what's good is whole unpraised. Do less: only what's necessary. All gone: Vespasian's Rome. And now the headland. Each one takes a weight off: the weight of later, of comparison, of credit, of praise, of busyness, of urgency. What's left, after all that, is something like a rock in the sea. Not hard. Just steady.
screen: `BE LIKE THE PROMONTORY.` · `THE WAVES BREAK CONTINUALLY.` · `IT STANDS, AND THE WATER SETTLES.` · `A WEEK OF WEIGHTS SET DOWN.` · then, large: `THE HEADLAND.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Sit as if you were a headland: feet heavy, back tall, shoulders loose. Now let one wave come: a frustration from this week. Let it hit. Notice the spray, the heat, the urge to push back. Don't push back. Don't move. Just breathe, and watch the wave slide away. If another comes, let it break too. Stand still through one wave. The bell holds the time.
The headland. Marcus says be like the promontory the waves keep breaking on: it stands firm, and the water calms around it. Today's word.
Your line: spray flies up and falls back. When a wave hits today, a word, a mood, a piece of news, stand still through it, and let it settle on its own. Day five hundred sixty.

fork.reveal: Marcus's headland neither fights nor flees: it stands, and the fury of the water calms around it.

original.note: Greek, 'height, headland, cape': the rock Marcus tells himself to be like in 4.49.

trapdoor: what you thought: be tough.
what it means: be steady; the waves keep coming, and by not moving you let them settle.
what a scholar hears: akra, a high point or cape; the same root gives the Acropolis, the 'high city' of Athens.
